extracted.intended_audience: agency policymakers, e-rulemaking platform designers, open-government researchers, and advocates of public participation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and evaluating Rulemaking 2.0 systems (web platforms and processes) that support broader, better public participation in federal rulemaking by adapting Web 2.0 technologies, human supports, and evaluation methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposefully adapt Web 2.0 technologies and methods to lower participation barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking 2.0 must recognize the several barriers to making rulemaking more broadly participatory, and purposefully adapt Web 2.0 technologies and methods to lower those barriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should not assume off-the-shelf social-web tools will suffice; instead they must select and adapt technologies and interaction methods specifically to reduce the obstacles that keep citizens from participating in rulemaking. The platform should be engineered with the explicit goal of lowering barriers rather than merely providing a forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address ignorance of the rulemaking process
rubrics_metrics.description: Broader, better public participation is hampered by ignorance of the rulemaking process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems should include educational content, explanations, and scaffolding that teach users how rulemaking works and what meaningful participation requires. Antipattern: assuming users understand procedural norms, deadlines, or the significance of different parts of rule materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase public awareness of ongoing rulemakings of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation is limited by unawareness that rulemakings of interest are going on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms should provide discovery, targeted outreach, and notification mechanisms so potential participants learn which rulemakings are relevant to them. Examples include topic-based alerts, searchable catalogs, and channels that surface timely opportunities to comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigate information overload from length and complexity of materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Broader participation is hampered by information overload from the length and complexity of rulemaking materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide summaries, issue maps, plain-language explanations, and tools to navigate and digest long regulatory texts. Anti-pattern: presenting raw rule documents without synthesis, annotation, or guided reading aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide the right mix of technology, content, and human assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: To be effective, a Rulemaking 2.0 system must provide the right mix of technology, content, and human assistance to support users in the unfamiliar environment of complex government policymaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine automated tools (e.g., classifiers, summarizers), curated content (e.g., contextual explanations, plain-language summaries), and human moderators or facilitators who can guide participants, answer questions, and help translate public input into usable formats for agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate human and computer support for public comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation Room uses selected live rulemakings to experiment with human and computer support for public comment; Rulemaking 2.0 systems should similarly combine both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments and workflows that let computational methods augment human judgment (e.g., clustering comments, surfacing representative views) while human actors provide interpretation, synthesis, and quality control. Evaluate hybrids in live settings to refine the balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate analogies to common Web services
rubrics_metrics.description: No existing, commonly used Web services or applications are good analogies for what a Rulemaking 2.0 system must do to lower these barriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not simply copy features from social media or consumer web apps without adapting them for the special demands of rulemaking (complex documents, procedural requirements, and civic stakes). Design decisions should be driven by the unique tasks of deliberation, civic input, and policy-making support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground design strategies in theory and test them in practice (evidence-based design)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate project goal is to provide guidance on design, technological, and human intervention strategies, grounded in theory and tested in practice, for effective Rulemaking 2.0 systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop interventions informed by theory (e.g., participation barriers, information design) and evaluate them via pilots (like Regulation Room). Use empirical results to iterate on design; measure outcomes such as participation rates, quality of comments, and usability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spur users to revise expectations about web engagement and civic participation
rubrics_metrics.description: The system must also spur users to revise their expectations about how they engage information on the Web and, perhaps, about what is required for civic participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design UX and interaction flows that encourage deeper engagement (e.g., prompting users to read summaries before commenting, showing impact of input). Consider features that socialize norms of meaningful participation rather than enabling shallow or performative comments.
